Through sheer determination, overwhelming preparation, and hard work, the Prime Minister has managed to achieve a momentous agreement in principle to changes to the Constitution. The provinces have gained new powers in many areas, including a voice in the reform of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Supreme Court. subsubtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL OPERATIONS WORKERS-VOTE IN FAVOUR OF UNIONIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to draw the attention of the House to an historic moment in our history yesterday when Parliament Hill employees voted to join the union of their choice, the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
In a certification vote for which 537 employees were eligible, 82 per cent voted, and 72 per cent voted in favour of joining the Parliament Hill local of the PSAC. This overwhelming endorsement for the union demonstrates that the men and women who serve this institution so faithfully wish to have the same representation right which is granted to, and taken for granted by, so many Canadian workers.
The certification is the culmination of a five-year struggle to establish the collective bargaining rights of workers on Parliament Hill. Members of the NDP salute the persistence and patience these workers have shown in their efforts to establish their union. I fully expect these negotiations to be successful and to be followed by many others as all eligible staff on the Hill exercise their collective bargaining rights in the years to come.

Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to report to the House on the meeting of First Ministers yesterday at Meech Lake. I am honoured to inform the House that at about 10 p.m last night the Premiers and I reached unanimous agreement in principle on a constitutional package which will allow Quebec to rejoin the Canadian constitutional family.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
This agreement enhances the Confederation bargain and strengthens, I believe, the federal nature of Canada. Although it remains to be formalized, it represents in the judgment of First Ministers from all political stripes and from all areas of the country an historic accomplishment.
The Meech Lake Agreement springs from the Canadian tradition of honourable compromise and is a tribute to the statesmanship and leadership that all First Ministers demonstrated yesterday at Meech Lake. Our task, simply put, was to settle a constitutional impasse which was incompletely resolved in 1981. Our task was to attempt to reconcile Quebec's distinct needs with the interests of all other provinces and the good of the country as a whole.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, at this time I am pleased to table the statement of principles that constitute the Meech Lake Agreement.
The essence of the agreement is as follows: We agreed to recognize the distinctiveness Quebec brings to Canada, which includes within it two main linguistic communities.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We agreed to give constitutional protection to an expanded immigration agreement with Quebec and to enter into accords with other provinces, appropriate to their circumstances.
We agreed to entrench the Supreme Court of Canada and the requirement that at least three of the nine justices appointed be from Quebec, and to provide for provincial involvement in Supreme Court appointments.
We agreed that reasonable compensation be granted to provinces that do not participate in future national shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, if they undertake their own initiatives or programs compatible with national objectives.
May 1, 1987

We agreed that all provinces must approve changes to national institutions under Section 42 of the 1982 Constitution act, and that the Government of Canada will provide reasonable compensation in all cases where a province opts out of an amendment transferring provincial jurisdiction to Parliament.

We agreed that there will be annual First Ministers' Conferences on the Constitution and that the first will be held before the end of 1988 to discuss Senate reform, the fisheries and other items to be agreed upon. Until Senate reform is achieved appointments to the Senate will be made by the federal Government from lists of candidates furnished by the provinces. We are also entrenching in the Constitution the annual First Ministers' Conference on the Economy.

Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Agreement is good for Canada, and good for Canadians.
It will unblock the constitutional reform process and enable Canadians to turn their attention to other issues such as Senate reform and fisheries.
Mr. Speaker, this agreement represents the best features of a vital federal system, one which 1 believe responds to the aspirations of Canadians in every corner of the country.
It reflects a spirit of partnership-and not one of endless federal-provincial power struggles.
The work of nation-building goes on. Shortly, officials will begin drafting a constitutional text which will reflect the Meech Lake Agreement. I shall be convening a conference of First Ministers within weeks, the purpose of which will be to seek formal agreement. On the assumption that a formal agreement is reached at the conference, the constitutional amending process will proceed. An amending resolution will be tabled in Parliament and in the legislative assembly of each province. Proclamation will follow once all the resolutions have been approved.
Mr. Speaker, Sir Wilfrid Laurier once said:
The governing motive of my life has been to harmonize the diverse elements
which compose our country.
Surely, that is the wish of every Member on all sides of the House. That is our policy, our purpose-building a stronger Canada for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I congratulate the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) as well as Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa and the other provincial premiers for their constructive work and the result achieved yesterday.
Statements by Ministers
It is a happy day for Canada and for Quebec, particularly for all those who believed that our country would remain united by respecting the diversity of its regions and the equality of its citizens.
I have always believed that it was essential to the future of our country that Quebec be a major and leading partner of the Canadian Federation and a full-fledged participant in its evolution.
That is what I stated in an interview with Le Devoir in June 1986, and what has led the Liberal Party of Canada to adopt, at its convention last November a clear position on the place of Quebec within the constitutional agreement of 1982.
I must tell the House that the constructive work of the Liberal Opposition and of the New Democratic Party did contribute to create a favourable atmosphere and context for agreement.
Our Party held a democratic debate on a resolution dealing with each point of the agreement, and thus we showed that a national Party, with representatives of all regions of Canada, could reach a firm consensus which could be a reasonable basis for an agreement.
In addition, we refrained from politicizing this question in the House of Commons. I, as much as the Members of the Official Opposition and the New Democrats purposely avoided embarrassing the Government about this issue. We knew that the provincial premiers and the representatives of the Canadian Government were studying the views set forth by Quebec, and that it was desirable that the interests of the country take precedence over partisan considerations.
Also, we must admit that Quebec is led by a Government which is openly federalist, nationalist but federalist, and which believes in the future of our country. It is a Government which is inspired by positive nationalism, which is aware that there is a way to conciliate and reconcile the objectives of the preservation and defence of the French language and culture while guaranteeing minority rights.
I was also advised that the Premier of Ontario played a leading role in the definition of a consensus, a fact I should like to emphasize in this House.
I just heard about the agreement-I didn't have time to read the text on my way back from Montreal this morning-so I am not in a position to comment on the contents. However, I will say that recognition of Canada's linguistic duality, of Quebec's distinct position as the main, but not exclusive, source of French language and culture in this country, and of the multicultural character of Canadian society would seem to be a sound foundation on which to build our future.
A more specific definition of powers with respect to immigration will guarantee that Quebec and other provinces, if they so desire, will be in a position to enhance the balance between language groups.

May 1, 1987
Statements by Ministers
The amending formula should also be changed to provide explicit guarantees that the status of federal institutions will not be modified without the consent of Quebec and the other provinces. In other words, the national interest must be served.
I would have to read the text. Perhaps the formula is too rigid for the future. We will have to look at this very closely.
We have recognized that spending authority is also a major concern. We intend to take a positive approach to the proposed text, while bearing in mind that because of this authority, Canada has today a social security and income support system that is among the most progressive in the world and the envy of many countries.
We shall therefore wish to ensure that nothing in the future will prevent the Government of Canada from improving the lot of medium-and low-income Canadians and to take action to guarantee greater social justice and equal opportunities for all Canadians.
The history of our country shows that our nation has evolved thanks to the reasonable nature of the aspirations of its citizens and the legitimate claims of both federal and provincial Governments.
This agreement will not be the last in our history. More progress can be achieved in relation with Senate reform and a clearer definition of some of the powers shared by the two levels of Government.
However, we recognize that, by taking its rightful place at the constitutional table, Quebec will continue to act as a catalyst for change and progress, and that there is some hope a better definition of the status of native Canadians can finally be achieved.
It is in this spirit, Mr. Speaker, that we shall take part in the coming debate on the resolution which must be passed by this House to implement the agreement reached by the Prime Minister of Canada and the provincial premiers.

In commending the Prime Minister and his colleagues, the First Ministers of the provinces, I want to say to him that the work accomplished yesterday was encouraging and constructive for the country. Bringing Quebec into our constitutional fabric, fully into the Canadian family, was an objective worth his time and worth the time of the First Ministers. We are very encouraged by the result.
I have not had an opportunity, nor have my colleagues, to study the text. As I said in French, I came back from Montreal when I learned that the Prime Minister would be making a statement this morning. We will, of course, have some questions to put to him and to the Government.
We are concerned, first, about the limitations on the spending power. Do they preclude national programs? Does this mean that in future a national child care program is impossible? What about a guaranteed annual income? Would
medicare have been possible under the agreement now contemplated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the provincial Premiers, or unemployment insurance for that matter? We will want to study the text of the spending power very carefully.
How will the expansion of opting out with compensation affect the quality of services and the uniformity of services in Canada? Who will decide national objectives? Senate reform will now require unanimous approval. Maybe the amending formula, even affecting federal institutions, will be too tight and too rigid. Until that formula is resolved, of course, and until Senate reform becomes a fact, we now understand that the provinces will submit lists of potential Senators to the Prime Minister. There are a lot of sad faces over there, Mr. Speaker.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think they have taken it very well this morning.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Are we now, however, in a constitutional strait-jacket? Will we ever really see Senate reform? Will we ever see an elected Senate under the formula agreed upon between the Prime Minister and the provincial Premiers?
We will want to study, the language of the distinctive character of Quebec. Will it be in the preamble? Will it be in the body of the Constitution? Do we yet know how widely it will influence the interpretation of that Constitution?
The Prime Minister seems to have accommodated many provincial concerns. That is the reason for the success, I am sure, of the negotiations. We will want to know from him what the federal Government got in return and what it sought. Did it seek changes to Section 23, the minority language rights feature of the Charter? Did it seek to eliminate the "notwithstanding clause", Section 33? If these questions were not raised at Meech Lake, will they be raised before the final deal is signed?
The Constitution requires, obviously, parliamentary assent to the text as it is eventually drafted. The Prime Minister must bring that before Parliament, as the Premier of Quebec must bring it before the Assemblee Nationale and as the other provincial premiers must bring it before their respective legislatures.
Will this Parliament have an opportunity to debate these issues before the final test is negotiated and signed? It is clear that Parliament will have to approve whatever the final text is in order to give it constitutional validity, as will provincial legislatures. My question to the Prime Minister, which we will pursue over the forthcoming days is, will this Parliament have an opportunity for some input into the final text before it is finally signed?
May 1, 1987

That being said, Mr. Speaker, it is a notable day for Canada. The Prime Minister deserves to enjoy his weekend, despite some of the events that will be happening; but for today it is a very significant accomplishment.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as someone who has participated in this House in the process of constitutional change in recent years, I do know something about the immense difficulties, in a country of our nature, that are involved for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the other Premiers of our nation. I too want to begin my comments by complimenting the Prime Minister and the Premiers for reaching an Accord that I hope will be seen, after final analysis, to be something that all of Canada can cherish.
Hear, hear!

Constitutional change is always a difficult process, especially in our country with its great economic and cultural diversity. In Canada, we must be sensitive to the needs of assuring adequate powers to provincial governments so that they can meet the needs of their quite different regions.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, there is a crucial necessity of ensuring that the power and the authority of the central Government is fully adequate, not only to carry out certain national functions important to all Canadians now, but also to be sufficient to enable the Government of Canada to initiate for the future in ways that can make our country even better. The need for a national child care program is a perfect current illustration of this point.

All Canadians know that the Premiers had the important and very special task of agreeing on proposals which would open the door to Quebec, the only province not to have signed the 1982 constitutional agreement.
The unique character of Quebec in Canada, the only province where the language and culture of the majority are French, is a fact which enriches the lives not only of Quebecers, but of all Canadians.
This fact must be recognized in the Canadian Constitution. Such is the policy of my Party.

The Prime Minister and the Premiers therefore had a very challenging task before them. All Canadians, I am sure, were pleased to hear that an agreement in principle was reached at Meech Lake last evening. The coming together of the Canadian family is desired by us all in this House and by all Parties and regions in our country. I compliment the Prime Minister
Statements by Ministers
and the Premiers representing such diverse regions, cultures and political Parties in reaching that agreement in principle.
I hope, like all Canadians, that when we see the fine print and study its implications our initial, genuine pleasure at the news of an accord will be sustainable. The Prime Minister will understand that my withholding of a complete endorsation of the agreement at this point is not at all churlish in nature, but rests entirely on the responsibility of my Party to study the details and the implications of what has been agreed upon. I deeply hope that such study will warrant wholehearted endorsation.
I would like to conclude with reference to one item in particular. In the accord, as the Prime Minister knows, there is a proposal to put in the Constitution specific commitments to meetings of the First Ministers on Senate reform and on economic matters. As one Canadian, 1 regret the complete absence of any reference to our aboriginal peoples. There was a conference, as the Prime Minister knows, that took place not long ago in this city in which we as a country and as political Parties failed to meet the needs and legitimate aspirations of our aboriginal peoples. I had hoped that there would have been a reference in the document that had been agreed upon to a commitment to carry on with such conferences in the future until the legitimate aspirations of our aboriginal peoples have been met.
I conclude, as I began, on a positive note, Mr. Speaker. I congratulate the Prime Minister and the First Ministers on this new beginning, and hope that when we see the final wording it will be an historic day indeed, and one that all of us will be able to look back upon with pride and with pleasure.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee, and Motion No. 12 (Mr. Orlikow, p.4936).

Mr. Speaker, as the House will recall, I was defending Motion No. 12 when the debate last ended some weeks ago, and I believe I have four or five minutes remaining.
I should like to remind the House what is at issue with Motion No. 12. Basically what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has in mind is commendable. In his motion he is proposing to put in place in Bill C-22 a recommendation of Mr. Eastman who, in his testimony before the committee, pointed out that there were three shortcomings in the legislation. I will just review them very quickly.
The first one in his opinion was that we should allow the research and development ratio of individual firms to be revealed. His suggestions were ways of improving the legislation, so he was hoping the R and D ratio would be revealed. The second one was that the board should remove, if need be, the exemption from compulsory licensing from all the patents of firms with excessive prices, a power which is not in Bill C-22. His third recommendation, with which the amendment deals specifically, was to reconsider the transitional arrangements and allow firms which have compulsory licences to exercise them when they receive a notice of compliance. This amendment proposes to do precisely that.
As you will know, Mr. Speaker, because you have been following the debate very carefully, 153 applications were caught when the Government decided to stop the issuance of further licences or notices of compliance beyond July 27 of last year. I believe I mentioned to the House earlier that one of those drugs was a generic drug to take the place of the ulcer drug Zantac.
I also pointed out some of the economic advantages to the users of such drugs.
The Canadian Association of Consumers and the New Democratic Party feel that it is unfair and unreasonable for these 153 applications for licence to be stopped simply by a ukase from the Minister performing the ancient function of his art. The result will be much higher drug prices for consumers who will not have access to these 153 generic drugs which were on their way to being made available to Canadian consumers.
Motion No. 12 would correct that situation and would allow all these 153 applications, which are part way through the system, to be accepted and to receive a licence or a notice of compliance to make them available to the public.
In closing, I point out to Hon. Members of the government Party, who do not seem to be too interested in supporting this motion up to this point in time, that in effect Bill C-22 is retroactive legislation. I remind the older members of the Government who were here during the last Parliament that they made that particular point loudly and clearly. They rang bells and stormed the Speaker's chair as a result of a retroactive clause which was as reprehensible when the Liberals did it as it is when the Conservatives are proposing to do it.
I hope they recall their earlier rationalization and apply it to clear up this shortcoming in the Bill and to do away with an attempt by the Government to introduce what is in effect retroactive legislation. I plead for support for Motion No. 12.

He said: Mr. Speaker, in my view this is a very important amendment. It might well be called the "Michel Cote clause" or, better still, the "C. Joe Stettler clause".
Everyone who has followed the progress of this Bill knows of the great changes which occurred over the summer of 1986 after the Bill was almost introduced by the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on June 27, 1986, and was finally introduced by the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) on November 7, 1986.
There were several changes to the Bill, and three of them significantly weakened it. What was dropped were the requirements of manufacturers to manufacture in Canada in order to keep exclusivity. The penalty clause was softened for excessive prices, and the criteria used by the drug prices review board were significantly weakened by making the costs of
Patent Act
making and marketing drugs a secondary criterion for determining costs.
What our amendment does is bring back the original clause in its entirety. For those who would like to see a Canadian drug manufacturing industry as opposed to one that exclusively imports its active ingredients, this amendment is worthy of support.
Attention was drawn to the matter when C. Joe Stettler, the head of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of the United States, disclosed on The Journal television program that he knew the previous Bill had been substantially changed or "toned down", as he put it.
Since the interview had been filmed a week before Bill C-22 was introduced, the question naturally became, how did he know? The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs kept insisting that he had never met with or never heard of C. Joe Stettler, and neither had his department.
Of course C. Joe Stettler does not have to bother to know the Minister. He can simply get the same information through his client organization in Canada, the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, which is well connected enough to hire the likes of Government Consultants International and even the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in the Liberal Government, Judy Erola, so that this information is supplied to him with no fuss or protocol.
However, the lasting impression about the incident is that the Bill is being significantly influenced, if not written, in the United States. The Minister can maintain, as he does, that he knows of no U.S. influence on him, but the features of the legislation have been so shaped that the benefits are accruing to U.S.-based companies and the costs are being paid by Canadians.
Let me digress for a moment to point out to the Minister the objections made to the Bill by hundreds of organizations representing hundreds of thousands of people, despite the protestations of the Minister that they did not really understand what was involved. Despite all the pledges of the Minister that this Bill when enacted would not substantially increase the cost of drugs to ordinary people, until today they have been rejected by most of those organizations.
1 would like to read from a letter sent to the present Minister by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. This letter was written on April 22, 1987, and the bishops had this to say:
On behalf of the Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops we wish to express our concern over changes to the Drug Patent Act (Bill C-22).
We have followed the debate on this legislation and have noted that the pressure to change Canada's generic drug laws has not come from the people of this country. Indeed, national organizations representing thousands of Canadians from virtually all sectors of society have been unanimous in calling upon your Government not to proceed with the proposed legislation.

May 1, 1987

We add our voice to that call because we believe that this legislation, if enacted, would have detrimental effects on average Canadians, especially on the elderly and the poor. Thanks in large part to existing drug patent legislation, Canadians enjoy low prescription drugs prices and high standards of health care.
The proposed amendments will cost Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars annually in drug price increases. The changes will also have serious implications for health care costs and for the future of Medicare in this country.
We urge your government to resist the pressure from the multinational drug industry and from the United States Administration. At the moment in history when your government is negotiating a bilateral free trade arrangement with the United States, the people of Canada are watching vigilantly to ensure that the interests of the common good of the Canadian people are not sacrificed to market interests.
i will not continue reading because of time limitations.
That letter was signed by Paul J. O'Byrne, Bishop of Calgary, Chairman of the Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs. I hope the Minister will take the time to tell us his reply to that Bishop of the Catholic Church speaking for all the bishops, a bishop from his own city.
Just last week hearings were held by a committee of the United States House of Representatives which deals with questions of health. Let me read a couple of paragraphs from the report on that, which appeared in The Globe and Mail of April 22, 1987:
Witnesses praised and condemned Canada's system during the hearing at which Harry Eastman, the Toronto economist who led a Canadian inquiry into the subject, testified that Canada's current rules have saved drug consumers millions of dollars.
Let me digress to point out to the Minister again that Professor Eastman has said repeatedly that the system we have in place has saved Canadians many millions of dollars. The article goes on:
Subcommittee staff prepared a report showing that prescription drug prices in the United States have increased more than 79 per cent during the past six years and that the industry has spent only one of every three dollars from that increase on research and development...
The consumer-oriented American Association of Retired Persons, however, praised the Canadian system as "an appropriate market-oriented model for moderating the trend in escalating prescription drug prices."
I say to the Minister that, as we have said all along, the Bill the Government is forcing through the House despite the representations of dozens of organizations will be a major blow to ordinary Canadians.
Let me return for a moment to the statement made by the former Minister in praise of the new policy of his Government. I quote from his press statement of June 27, 1986:
Here are the specific changes we propose: patent-holding pharmaceutical firms in Canada will receive a phased-in period of exclusivity ranging from seven to 10 years. This, let me point out, is still less than the full patent protection which applies to other products.
In order to be assured of this exclusivity, however, an innovative firm must manufacture the fine-chemical ingredients in Canada . .. While the previous policy encouraged the importation of fine chemicals, our new policy will encourage their direct manufacture in Canada.
That provision was disposed of between the time the former Minister proposed to introduce the Bill and the time the present Minister brought the Bill in. It went because the American Government put the pressure on the Minister and the Government caved in.
We say that this Bill is wrong. The amendment I have moved would improve the Bill and I would urge Hon. Members to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to this amendment to Bill C-22 moved by my colleague from the New Democratic Party. In the few moments I have before you call it 1.23, Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that the intent of this particular amendment is to try to facilitate, as best one can under these very adverse circumstances, a Canadian pharmaceutical industry predicated on the viability of Canadian-owned firms.
As it now stands, the legislation makes it very easy for multinational corporations to come to Canada to participate in the pharmaceutical sector of the economy. 1 think the over-all objective of any public legislation, particularly when dealing with pharmaceuticals, ought to be to build on the pillars of a public policy. I feel that one of these pillars is that we provide fair prices to Canadian consumers, whether they be the sick, the elderly, the poor or those on fixed incomes.
Fair prices for Canadian consumers is one such pillar, but we should also try to provide incentives to those individuals who are trained in a profession. We want them to reap some of the benefits of their innovative works. As well, real dollars should be directed into research and development in Canada, not just mere quotations from the newspapers about the lofty intentions of multinational corporations.
In my view, another such pillar must be the facilitation of the development of a Canadian pharamaceutical industry. I think it is fair to say that there is not a country in the world that has developed a viable pharmaceutical industry based solely on the existence and operation of multinational corporations. In this instance we have an opportunity to facilitate with reason, as always, a Canadian pharmaceutical industry. I know that I, as well as Members opposite and Members to the left, can fully appreciate that Canada is not a major player in the world market. However, that should not lessen our will and desire to try and enhance our own pharmaceutical industry.
I think the amendment attempts to do that in a number of ways. Yet the Government, for whatever reasons, some of which have been alluded to and some of which have not, is reluctant to reward Canadian entrepreneurs, reluctant to give them a legislative framework to assist and enhance their opportunities in a Canadian market. If it did, that could very well mean Canadians would become leaders in this sector. Then they, too, would be able to export their products as well as the technology which went into formulating the various new drugs. The Government consistently and persistently refuses to try and assist in developing a policy along those lines.
In November of 1986 the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) said that for the previous four months he had an opportunity to fully review the draft legislation. He had consulted many interested parties and was
May I, 1987

convinced of its merits. The thrust of this Bill is the same as that announced in June with some modifications which I will refer to later. The Bill that the Government attempted to introduce in June had a few provisions which are not in the present Bill. However, it is very clear to all Members of Parliament that the philosophy behind the Bill is that of a giveaway of our pharmaceutical industry to multinational corporations wherever they may be based.
I note it is 1.23 p.m. I hope I can resume debate at two o'clock under your chairmanship.

Mr. Speaker, I support the motion of my colleague from the New Democratic Party. In the few minutes I have I want to reiterate for Members opposite that we must be concerned and must be prepared to take concrete and specific actions with regard to Canadianizing our pharmaceutical industry.
It is well and good to say that Canada must abide by certain international conventions, whether the Paris Convention of 1904 or the subsequent treaties with regard to the issue of intellectual property rights, but it should be noted that since that time many countries have taken it upon themselves to try to develop their own pharmaceutical industry based upon their human resources, and also to use the state as an instrument of public policy to achieve their objectives.
In this instance the Government of the day, as many have argued, is trying to appease its neighbours to the south. As I indicated last night on the debate on the farm crisis, I am not anti-American. I want to make that perfectly clear. I have great difficulties with the American administration, but I am not anti-American. It seems that in our dealings with that country we in Canada always seem to be taking it in the neck.
I think this is a prime example of a case in which Canada has consented, both intellectually and in practice, to the wishes of our friends to the south, thereby giving multinational corporations in the United States and elsewhere everything they have asked for while we in Canada are failing to achieve the goals and objectives which are necessary to make the Canadian economy vibrant and viable.
In the minute which I have remaining I want to congratulate my colleague from the New Democratic Party who put forward this amendment. As was said in the Committee on Bill C-22 which studied this legislation, it would have been nice if Members opposite had been in agreement with the objectives which we laid out so early in our deliberations. As time has
Patent Act
progressed we have seen that the Government is falling prey to multinational corporations. I suggest, with great respect to you, Sir, that that may very well not be in Canada's best interests, particularly in the long term.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of Motion No. 14 placed before the House by my hon. friend, the Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). It is a fairly substantial amendment which attempts to rectify some of the shortcomings of this Bill and bring back the rights of the generic drug industry to enable it to continue to operate as it did prior to the Government's decision of last July to stop 153 applications which were in the process of being accepted for additional generic drugs.
This entire exercise by the Opposition has been aimed at keeping down the cost of drugs to Canadians. The policy put into effect in the mid-1970s in this country to allow the manufacturing, under compulsory licence, of generic drugs has attracted attention around the world from consumers and health care personnel. It has been widely accepted as a good thing for the health care system in Canada as it provides relatively new patented inventions to consumers at a low cost. It also provided some protection to the patent holder because of the compulsory licence feature.
This initiative has attracted the attention of a wide range of Canadian society beyond the consumer association and some of the health care groups. It has attracted the attention of farm organizations like the Keystone Agricultural Producers in Manitoba, who have written to all Members of Parliament pointing out that the existing generic drug law has been good for Canadian rural residents. The Keystone Agricultural Producers speak on behalf of farmers and their families and point out that they have a double concern about what they believe is a flawed initiative.
They believe, as consumers of health services and drugs, that the generic drug law should remain as is and that the changes proposed in Bill C-22 should be dropped.
Their second concern as agricultural producers who use farm chemicals is that it has been a long-standing effort by farmers, through their organizations, to attempt to have on equivalent generic drug law and compulsory licensing for farm chemicals that they require in order to maintain the high productivity of Canadian farms.
The Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Agriculture has taken upon itself a special project to investigate farm input costs. One of those input costs that has received substantial attention has been farm chemicals and veterinary drugs. Virtually without exception, the witnesses who appeared before us said that from the farmer's point of view the farm chemical industry needs some legislation similar to the generic drug law so that there could be compulsory licences applied to farm chemicals. Some have also indicated that this should be extended to include veterinary medicines. These submissions to the committee point out that the farm community has a parallel concern in this area.

I also have a letter from the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, signed by Paul J. O'Byrne, Bishop of Calgary, Chairman of Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs. Tie has addressed the letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Leaders of the opposition Parties and numerous Members of Parliament. He points out:
On behalf of the Episcopal Commission for Social Affairs of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops we wish to express our concern over changes to the Drug Patent Act (Bill C-22).
We have followed the debate on this legislation and have noted that the pressure to change Canada's generic drug laws has not come from the people of this country.
Indeed, national organizations representing thousands of Canadians from virtually all sectors of society have been unanimous in calling upon your government not to proceed with the proposed legislation.
That is, in fact, the case. No Canadian organization or group loudly called for these kinds of changes. The change seems to have come from south of the border where there is considerable pressure placed on the Prime Minister and his Government to create a legislative level playing field so that our drug laws more closely resemble those of the United States as a forerunner to a free trade arrangement between the two countries.
The letter continues:
We add our voice to that call because we believe that this legislation, if enacted, would have detrimental effects on average Canadians, especially on the elderly and the poor.
Thanks in large part to existing drug patent legislation, Canadians enjoy low prescription drug prices and high standards of health care. The proposed amendments will cost Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars annually in drug price increases. The changes will also have serious implications for health care costs and for the future of medicare in this country.
This point has been made by many groups and individuals across the country. It is not only the opinion of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, whose letter I am reading now. It goes on:
We urge your Government to resist the pressure from the multinational drug industry and from the United States administration. At the moment in history when your Government is negotiating a bilateral free trade arrangement with the United States, the people of Canada are watching vigilantly to ensure that the interests of the common good of the Canadian people are not sacrificed to market interests.
As the federal Commission of Inquiry on the Pharmaceutical Industry declared in its 1985 report, the Canadian compulsory licensing policy "can be thought of as a mechanism to provide socially optimal patent protection in the pharmaceutical industry that other countries might well emulate".
Because the people of Canada affirm that this policy is not-and should never become-a trade issue, we urge you, in the name of Canada's most vulnerable citizens, to withdraw Bill C-22.
I believe the bishop has expressed the sentiments of hundreds of other Canadians, groups and institutions that have appeared before the committee, presented briefs, and written letters to individual Members of Parliament. The House will know that we have received petitions from hundreds of Canadians who have urged the Government to give up its
effort to push through Bill C-22. I urge government Members to support this motion and reconsider the Government's decision to put forward Bill C-22.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House this afternoon to deal very briefly with Motion No. 14 which was moved by our NPD colleagues. I feel it is a major otion because it would change significantly the Bill introduced in the House by the minister.

This amendment should probably be referred to as the Joe Stettler clause, because we know that the Bill went through great changes after the initial flawed attempt of the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Member for Langelier (Mr. Cote).
I remember the day when he was sitting at that end of the House and tried to introduce his Bill, but forgot the required Royal documentation necessary to present the Bill. This mistake was probably caused by the fact that he spent too much time that day at the press conference across the street and not enough time concentrating on what he should have been doing in the House.
Nevertheless, after that flawed attempt by the Government to introduce the Bill at that time, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) brought the Bill in. It came out differently than the Bill of his predecessor. Mr. C. Joe Stettler, the head of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association, not of Canada but of the United States, said on The Journal television program that he knew the previous Bill had been substantially changed or, as he said "toned down". It is interesting, of course, that no one in Canada knew that but someone in the United States knew it well.

As Canadians, Mr. Speaker, we should ask ourselves what are we here for. Have we been elected to the House of Commons of Canada to protect the interests of Mr. C. Joe Stettler, President of the Association of Drug Manufacturers of America, or those of Canadians?

That Bill C-22, be amended in Clause 15 by adding immediately after line 15
at page 13 the following:
"(3) Subsection 41.14(1) does not apply in respect of any licence or application for licence under Section 41 where the Commissioner finds that the licence that has been obtained or is sought by a person is necessary to the utilization, for the manufacture and sale of a medicine, of a biological process patented by the person, or for which a patent has been applied, and the process has been invented and developed by the person in Canada to such extent as is prescribed."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment could well be called the "Cangene amendment" because it was inspired and suggested by a representative of Cangene, which is a new and successful Canadian biotechnology company located in Mississauga, Ontario. Hon. Members should know that we do not have very many biotechnology companies and even fewer successful biotechnology companies.
In an appearance before the committee, the officers of Cangene pointed out that they had organized and prospered so far under the present Canadian patent law and they now feared that they would suffer greatly because of changes to the law being made by Bill C-22. It was another twist on the story of Canadian companies, such as the generic drug industry, being penalized in the future for having grown up under existing Canadian patent law. They were particularly concerned about the switch from patents on a process to patents on products, which is what this Bill, if it passes, will do.

May 1, 1987
Patent Act
In the words of Dr. Robert Garvin, the vice-president for Research and Development at Cangene:
On the verge of our success, you propose to change the rules. Under the new rules, the Cangene process, already successful with one, perhaps successful with others yet to be tried, will be useless. It will be useless because you, in the amendments, will allow product patents. The natural health giving proteins will become the private property of a single company. The process used to make that protein, the Cangene process, will be immaterial.
Under your new rules or the rules proposed in the amendments, the battle for the market-place will move into the courtroom as it has in the United States. That will doom Cangene and Canada forever... from establishing a Canadian niche in the protein-based pharmaceutical manufacturing industry. Surely together we can write legislation which will not throw out the baby, Cangene, with the bath water.
That is what my amendment, Mr. Speaker, is trying to do. The committee was quite impressed with the presentation Cangene made and adopted an amendment to Section 41(1). It is meant to provide transitional arrangements for a period of four years in the case of microbiological processes intended for food and medicine.
This delay in the switch to product patents is to assist Cangene and other biotechnology companies to make the transition. However, this was only one of the proposals which Cangene made to the committee. Cangene also sees the value of compulsory licensing in its work, which is the purpose of the amendment brought forward here as Motion No. 16. It is restricted to the biotechnology area.
The purpose of the amendment is explained on page 14 of the Cangene brief to the legislative committee which dealt with Bill C-22. I quote from its submission:
The question still remains whether the prohibition of product patents in the biotechnology field would be sufficient to encourage the development of Canadian research and manufacturing firms such as Cangene. In Cangene's view, although such a change would be an enormous step forward, some aspects of compulsory licensing might still be necessary, because of the necessity in many instances to rely on enabling patents in order commercially to market a product. A patent rarely stands alone. Without some access to compulsory licensing, even though Cangene might own the patent to make human growth hormone by its own patented special process, the use of certain aspects of that process, or even the bottling of human growth hormone, might require access to patents not owned by Cangene and only available through licensing.
I could go on to quote further from the Cangene presentation. However, obviously, I do not have time.
I would like to put on the record some of the views which were outlined by Dr. Eastman in his report on which, supposedly, much of this legislation is based, although most of the recommendations he made have been ignored and rejected. I would like to quote from the section in his report which appears beginning on page 348 and which is entitled: "Compulsory Licensing and the Growth of Generic Production in Canada" in which he states:
The performance of the pharmaceutical industry in Canada does not differ significantly from that in other industrially advanced countries.
Its level of research and development is comparable to the disproportionately low level prevailing in such countries as Australia, Austria, Belgium,
Denmark, Finland, New Zealand, and the Netherlands. This contrasts with the very high level of research and development expenditures in France, West Germany, Japan, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. The structural characteristics of the industry are everywhere similar as are, in consequence, the incentives to which firms are subject, their behaviour, and their performance.
To stray for a moment from Professor Eastman's views, it is interesting to note that most of the countries he mentions, which are not doing any more than we are, do not have our laws. They have the laws to which we will move and which were in place before 1969. In those countries the industry is still not doing much in the way of research.
I would like to continue to quote from Professor Eastman's views. He stated:
Canadian federal policy, on the other hand, is indirect and seeks to affect the industry's performance by altering the conditions of competition at the manufacturers' level... That Canadian policy is currently all but unique among industrially advanced countries does not make it wrong. Indeed it can be thought of as a mechanism to provide socially optimal patent protection in the pharmaceutical industry that other countries might well emulate.
He then goes on to state:
The new policy of compulsory licensing to import gave rise to a vigorous and growing generic sector of the industry ... On the whole, compulsory licensing has caused no decline in the economic health of the patent-holding firms... Nevertheless, it is known that the generic sector was of negligible size in 1968 but contributed about 8 per cent of sales in 1983 and employed about 1,300 persons in 1982.
Professor Eastman concluded by stating:
However, it should be kept in mind that the generic sector grew to significance in the industry because of the profitability of compulsory licensing and might well not have obtained a share of the post-patent market without that base.
We see that Dr. Eastman's view is that compulsory licensing is the corner-stone for the generic industry and is part of a policy "that other countries might well emulate." By supporting the amendment which I am moving today the unique Canadian system of drug patents will be strengthened for biotechnology companies. Given the tremendous increase and the almost unbelievable explosion of new research and development in other countries, the few companies operating in this country need every bit of assistance they can get. That is why I am moving this amendment.

When Dr. Garvin, the Vice-President for Research and Development at Cangene, was before the committee he said this, and it is worth repeating because its importance will become obvious to Ministers and to Members of Parliament quite readily:

Here is a Canadian corporation operating in a new and innovative sector of our economy, the biotechnology industry, and prospering under the present legislation, the Patent Act as it now stands without any amendments thereto. The company was reasonably successful and hoping to make major break throughs. Yet the Government has come in and said, "We are going to change the rules of the game for Canadian corporations". Dr. Garvin went on further to state:
Under the new rules, the Cangene process, already successful with one and perhaps successful with others yet to be tried, will be useless. It will be useless, because you, in the amendments, will allow product patents. The natural health-giving proteins will become the private property of a single company. The process used to make that protein, the Cangene process, will be immaterial.
Under your new rules or the rules proposed in the amendments, the battle for the market-place will move into the courtroom, as it has in the United States. That will doom Cangene and Canada forever ... from establishing a Canadian niche in the protein-based pharmaceutical manufacturing industry. Surely together we can write legislation which will not throw out the baby, Cangene, with the bath water.
Patent Act
I come back to my initial intervention when I talked about the pillars of a Canadian pharmaceutical industry and the amendment submitted by my colleague on the left. You can see quite readily, Sir, that it is not merely opposition Members proposing amendments for the mere sake of debate. We have a legitimate corporation operating here in Canada with men and women employed in a very sophisticated complex industry who will now have their particular operation, if you will, cut because of the new changes in Bill C-22, hence the purpose of the amendment submitted by my colleague.
Again and again I must repeat, not for the purposes of trying to deafen Members opposite, who may be listening very carefully, but to try to irk them into rethinking and reconsidering their position with regard to the Patent Act and the pillars of developing a Canadian industry. This is one of them. I would have hoped that Members opposite would avail themselves of every opportunity to stand in the Chamber to support the amendment and the intent of it. As we have seen in the past, this has not been the case, Mr. Speaker.

I will have to put this in fast gear, then. These are amendments dealing primarily with the aspect of the operations of the Prices Review Board as set out in the legislation, Bill C-22. The motions that 1 have put forward, in particular Motion No. 17, require the industry to make quarterly reports to the board rather than at times at the discretion of the board. This significantly strengthens the watch-dog or monitoring capability of the board. Motion No. 18 allows the board outside of Canada to gather information on the cost of manufacturing medicines.
This amendment, in my view, has significant relevance with regard to the issue of transfer pricing, which 1 will speak about in a moment or two, and would allow the board to carry out meaningful investigation.
We have contended from day one that the prices review board as contained in the legislation is not constitutional. In questioning and in submitting a written argument to the Minister he refused to accept that argument. Having said that, there are some natural, in my view, amendments both substantive and consequential that ought to be in the Bill, or with the board anyway, even if it is found to be constitutional. That is a
question for the courts to decide at some point. Our fear in this Party is that the constitutionality of the board will be challenged by multinational corporations and they will use this as a lever to delay or to protract deliberations and activities of the board.
Having said all of that, Mr. Speaker, clearly if you do have a board, which seems from the perspective of my Party to be in absolute contradiction to the philosophy of the Members opposite, particularly the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Lewis), if the free market is to operate in Canada. I cannot for the life of me understand why the Conservative Government of the day would now want to put in the form of a regulation that the Prices Review Board monitor and advise on the pricing of pharmaceuticals in this country.
There seems to be a contradiction, because in 1983-84 the free market was advocated. In 1984 and in 1985 the free market was advocated. Now in 1986-87 it seems the reverse is advocated. I say that that is a contradiction. If the board is to be in place, if the courts do find it to be constitutional, it must have sufficient enabling powers within the substance and the make-up of the board to achieve the objective that it hopes to achieve.
If the board is to be limited to the parameters of Canada in terms of gathering information on the cost of what it will be for the manufacturing of the new drug, this in my view will prohibit and prevent the board from doing the job it was constituted to do originally, which is to advise and report on the cost of the manufacturing of the drug.
Many of these drugs in terms of ingredient, technology and the human resources that have gone into it may be located in various countries throughout the world. Canada has no leverage, no authority to say to multinational corporations who may be operating in Canada that we would like to see and have submitted an audited statement of the expenses and the expenditure program of the company in order to arrive at the figures they have quoted.
Why do 1 say that? It is because we were told in the legislative committee that it was upwards of $150 million to develop a new drug in Canada. I asked the multinational association, PMAC, to provide certain information on how it arrived at the cost of certain drugs. I was assured that 1 would receive that information, but 1 did not.
When I was in Washington 1 visited with the chairman of the subcommittee on environment and health which was conducting a study or investigation into the practising policies of pharmaceutical companies in the United States. We were led to believe from the information it had that the price was $50 million. When the chairman of a United States pharmaceutical organization was here in Canada, he was questioned on that matter at a press conference. I believe his statement indicated that it was something in the vicinity of $50 million for the manufacture of a new drug.
May 1, 1987

In order to get at the real cost of manufacturing a new drug, the board must have the powers in terms of being able to subpoena persons and information, wherever the information may be. However, as the legislation now stands, the board does not have the authority or jurisdiction to call for that information. If the Government is clear in its objectives, why would it want to hide the actual costs which go into developing and manufacturing new drugs?
Is it because the prices charged for particular drugs subsequent thereto will be very significant costs to senior citizens, the sick, the elderly, and those four million Canadians who have no drug program at all? If we knew the actual price predicated upon the information submitted, Canadians would have a better appreciation and understanding of why prices are what they are for certain drugs. I think it would be in their best interest to share that information with Canadians and with the board reviewing the prices, unless they want to hide it so that they can inflate their prices.
We are not trying to penalize anyone. We want to make certain that Canadian consumers will get a fair shake when it comes to the pricing of prescription drugs in Canada. These amendments would give the board a legislative authority and jurisdiction to obtain that information. At the present time the board does not have that authority.
We heard from a number of witnesses on the issue of transfer pricing. It is a very serious matter. Multinational corporations merely transfer prices from one jurisdiction to another. If the board does not have the authority to obtain that information, it will not be able to do the job which the Minister indicated he wanted it to do initially.
I hope Hon. Members will see the true value of these motions. I have not spoken on some of them because time is limited to 10 minutes at report stage. However, the amendments collectively would add immeasurably to the improvement of the Act if, on the hypothesis, that it is in fact constitutional.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of Motion No. 40 standing in my name which substitutes the following:
(c)	expenditures made by the patentee in Canada towards the cost of research and development relating to medicine; and;
(d)	expenditures to be made by the patentee in Canada towards the cost of research and development relating to medicine to the years 1990 and 1995 respectfully.
The reasons I have moved this amendment are fairly easy to understand for those who want to try to understand the problems confronting us in Bill C-22. We have seen the problems in Canada in getting companies to live up to commitments made to Governments for government assistance, Those difficulties are as old as the CPR, or more than 100 years, and as topical as the financial assistance given to the company which manufactures Coleco toys in Montreal that closed after receiving substantial federal grants.
Patent Act
In this legislation we have already had the example of the drug manufacturing clause being cut from the Bill which was introduced last June because multinational companies did not want to manufacture in Canada. The present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), not having manufacturing to talk about, has instead emphasized the commitment of companies to increase research in Canada. In his words, one of the objectives of Bill C-22 is:
To transform Canada's pharmaceutical sector into a world-class, innovative industry led by an unprecedented increase in investment and jobs in pharmaceutical research and development. The ratio of research to sales will double from the current level of under 5 per cent to 10 per cent by 1995, thereby directly creating an estimated 3,000 scientific and research related jobs and putting Canada at the forefront of leading nations in the pharmaceutical field.
Any person with an inquiring mind might be tempted to ask if we are being set up again with these promises.
After all, Dr. Eastman after his extensive studies in the pharmaceutical industry came to the following conclusion in his report:
In the Commission's opinion, Canada is not well placed to become a major world centre for pharmaceutical research or for the production of active chemical ingredients.
We should not be surprised at that conclusion of Dr. Eastman. We were told repeatedly by the companies themselves that to develop a completely new, important, and innovative drug would cost anywhere from $50 million to $100 million. Obviously no company would do that in Canada unless it has assurances that if it did the patent and manufacturing would not only be for Canada. We know that the multinational companies will do very little in that regard.
However, Dr. Eastman's caution did not stop the Minister. In the view of the Minister, the grounds for stating that Canada would become "at the forefront of leading nations" is based upon the following quote:
-extensive discussions with the innovative sector of the pharmaceutical industry from which the Government of Canada has received strong investment commitments .. . Specifically, the industry has undertaken to invest in Canada a growing percentage of sales revenues directly into R and D expenditures.
As a result of the policy change ... the industry is committed to increasing its current ratio of R and D to sales from 4.9 per cent to 8 per cent by 1990 and 10 per cent by 1995-a full doubling from the pre-policy level.
These commitments are not in the Bill. There is nothing in the Bill which would require the company to live up to these conditions, despite suggestions made by opposition Members and by many groups which appeared before the committee.
Since these commitments are not in the Bill, Dr. Eastman was forced to ask at committee for an amendment so that the drug prices review board could at least report the ratio of research and development to sales and the industry would know which ompanies were meeting their targets and which were not.

May 1, 1987
Patent Act
However, there is even more skepticism of a basic kind about the R and D commitments about which the Minister is so eager to talk. Paul Gorecki, an economist who worked on the Eastman Commission, told the committee the following:
Unfortunately it is difficult to evaluate these undertakings because no data is provided. Under what assumptions is the growth in R & D likely to occur? ... In the absence of answers to these questions and in view of the Commission's conclusions cited above one must unfortunately express skepticism about the projected doubling in R & D by 1995.
This amendment attempts to make the companies respond to the specific target years of 1990 and 1995. These are very important targets because if they are missed, reviews of the legislation can be triggered by Cabinet and by a parliamentary review.
There is the further controversy which has erupted over what constitutes R and D and what are really other kinds of research in marketing and clinical areas. We had long debates in committee about what constitutes research but, although we and many of the witnesses urged the Government to define research and development in the Bill, we were unable to convince the Government and it refused to do so.
The Minister's press release of December lists some 17 announcements totalling $770 million. Yet much of this money represents plant expansions that would be required in any case to serve a Canadian market that is doubling every five years. The research about which the Minister talked is clinical.
I would like to conclude by saying that we should remember what the Minister promised which was an expanded research effort which would create 3,000 scientific and research-related jobs and put Canada at the forefront of leading nations in the pharmaceutical field. That claim has its doubters, both over the number of jobs that will be created in scientific research and the quality of those jobs. That is what I am trying to pin down and get included in this Bill so we will really get the 3,000 jobs about which the Minister has spoken.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Cape Breton-East Richmond) moved:
speechtext:
Patent Act
Motion No. 19.
That Bill C-22, be amended in Clause 15 by striking out lines 12 to 14 at
page 14 and substituting the following therefor:
"(ii) any other patents of the patentee for inventions pertaining to medicine, whether granted".
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be brief. This amendment will put the Bill back into its June 1986 format regarding the powers of the board to repeal any of the patents held by a manufacturer sanctioned by the board. We must remember that the Government attempted to introduce draft legislation in June, 1986, but because of a procedural hiccup, it did not introduce it in accordance with the procedures of the House and thereafter introduced a Bill in the fall of 1986 in a somewhat different form from that of the original draft.
Instead of having the power to repeal only one patent, this amendment provides that the board would have the power to repeal patents that it had in the 1986 draft. This will significantly strengthen the powers of the board. There is no logical reason for this section of the Bill to have been removed by the Minister except pressure from brand name manufacturers. It makes no sense to weaken or reduce the enforcement options open to a regulatory body.
The board to which I have referred in earlier amendments to Bill C-22 has certain powers and one of the powers the board was to have according to the June 1986 draft was that, if it was found by the board on its determination that a company, multinational or otherwise, was in breach of the Bill, the board could exercise certain sanctions against the particular company in question. That particular company may have a number of patents and the board would have had the authority to remove those patents.
The legislation introduced subsequent to the June draft, the Bill that has been presented to the House by the Conservative administration, removes those sanctions. It allows the board to remove one patent without removing other patents. The authority the board may use in circumstances it deemed necessary has been relinquished. In my view and in the view of my Party, this certainly does not add to the functions or powers of the board.
By forming this board, we are acting as if it were to be used to make companies aware that if they breach the law or are in violation of pricing regulations, the board has the authority to remove those patents and so the companies would think twice. Their behaviour would be different. However, as the legislation is now written, a company that has 10 patents and is found to be gouging the public will have only one patent removed by the board because that is the only authority it has. We do not believe this is in the best interests of the administrative practices of the board.

May 1, 1987
Business of the House
I would think that regulatory agencies would want to have at their disposal a variety of sanctions they might impose. By restricting the board to only one action you restrict its effectiveness. If there was a violation, perhaps the penalty ought not to be the removal of that one patent. It may unduly affect the viability of the company concerned. Equally so, if a violation is of such significance that the only sanction available to the board is the removal of one patent, the board is again failing to achieve its objectives because it would not be allowed to remove more than one patent as may be called for a given significant violation.
This is not a mere partisan political issue. It is a fact of administrative law and regulatory practice that I would have thought Members opposite, particularly the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt), would subscribe to.
That is the pith and substance of this particular amendment. However, I again wish to recall for the benefit of the Chair that we still maintain that the constitutionality of this board will be challenged first and foremost by the multinational corporations. If the courts find they are constitutional, it would seem appropriate that the Government accept this amendment. If not, perhaps it should accept the argument and have the entire matter referred to the Supreme Court for adjudication of the constitutionality of this board.
I do not want to go on at length regarding the constitutionality because that issue will arise in a number of other motions and I know you will want to hear argument from all sides of the House on that matter.
Let me conclude with this. The Government is contradicting itself again and again. It advocated a free market and regulatory reform and it has now come full circle. It is doing away with compulsory licensing, which is a free market activity, so to speak. The Government is substituting regulation which it said it did not want. It talks about free market and is now intervening. I suggest that the law will not be effective the way it is drafted. Without this amendment it will be ineffective in attempting to achieve the goal of proper sanctions for those in violation of both the spirit and substance of the amendments to the Patent Act.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee, and Motion No. 19 (Mr. Dingwall, p. 5643).

Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 19, which we support, is almost identical to Motion No. 20 moved by the NDP. What it attempts to do is to reverse a Conservative change to the Bill which made a bad Bill worse. Back in June when the Government first attempted to introduce this very bad Bill it contained certain sanctions for drug companies which overcharged. The penalty was worded so that the patent was lost on any other patent of the patentee for an invention pertaining to medicine. In the November Bill, that was watered down to one other medicine. In other words, instead of losing all patents that pertain to medicine the company would lose only that which pertained to one other medicine.
That change reflects the influence which the American drug manufacturers have on the Canadian Government. It is a very clear illustration of the power of Mr. C. Joe Stettler, the well-paid and well-connected lobbyist on behalf of the PMA lobby in Washington. The fact that the Minister said he has never had a meeting with that lobbyist is incidental because the PMA is so well-connected here in Canada. It has its own lobbyists who were able to deliver the message to the Minister quite effectively.
In a CBC television interview which took place in advance of the tabling of the Bill in Parliament, Mr. Stettler was very forthcoming in pointing out to the Canadian public that changes had been made in the Bill in accordance with their desires. I would like to quote his words:
May I, 1987

Some of the penalties on violated pricing were pretty stiff and they were toned
down.
With this amendment we seek to return to the original wording in the June Bill. We would like to see a Bill which is not worse than it was originally intended to be. We would like to see a Bill which has not been interfered with to make it even more obnoxious to the Canadian people in order to satisfy the interests of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association in the U.S.
The U.S. companies now have a Bill they are very happy with, but it is not one that the Canadian people are going to be happy with. It will not in any way provide protection for them. It will result in higher prices for drugs and increased costs for provincial pharmacare programs. It is a vicious example of the way in which the Government bows down to the dictates of the American Government.
The very high percentage of foreign ownership of the Canadian drug industry is of major concern here. In 1981, of the 21 largest companies by sales, none was Canadian-owned. Foreign companies controlled about 92 per cent of the industry in 1972. Domestically owned companies supplied only 15 per cent of the Canadian pharmaceutical market in 1975 ranking us below countries such as Mexico, Iran, India and the Philippines. This information is from Dr. Joel Lexchin's book, The Real Pushers.
Between 1968 and 1979 the fraction of the Canadian market served by imports originating from parent countries or other subsidiaries abroad increased from 13.9 per cent of sales to 26.3 per cent while the fraction of the market served by the Canadian subsidiaries fell. Even in the late 1960s, drug manufacturing in Canada was minimal. Of all manufacturing, 85 per cent was confined to the conversion of imported material into final dosage form. In other words, we are taking the basic material manufactured abroad and only packaging it. That is the kind of manufacturing we did in the late 1960s. This is not good enough.
In addition, we should be aware of the extreme limitations which are put upon Canadian branch plants with respect to exporting abroad. Canada wants to be an exporting nation. We want to be able to export more than only wood products and grain products because we have a great deal of trouble with commodity prices. Presently Canadian branch plants in pharmaceuticals are not able to export because of foreign ownership and foreign control. Lexchin says:
The ability of Canadian branch plants to export drugs is also limited by foreign control. With most patents on drugs foreign-owned, subsidiary companies of the parent patentees control the market within their own jurisdictions. Export activity has to be confined to world areas where patents are not taken out; areas that are commercially insignificant. As a representative of a Canadian subsidiary in one U.S. company said, "We have so many plants all over the world 1 just do not know where we would export to."
Patent Act
This has led to the finding by the Department of Industry Trade and Commerce that Canadian subsidiaries are usually "not encouraged or permitted by the head office to assume responsibility for exports of their products". Our drug industry is dominated by foreign firms which dictated to the Canadian Government changes in legislation, which was wrong to begin with and worked against the interests of the Canadian public.
1 urge the Government to accept this amendment which restores the original wording of the section so that we do not have a bad Bill made worse through interference by the American Pharmaceutical Association, I hope all Members will consider the implications of this Bill and support this amendment.
