He said: Mr. Speaker, these motions deal primarily with the matter 1 raised earlier of the constitutionality of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board. Bill C-22 establishes a drug prices review board with a mandate to keep future prices of pharmaceuticals down. Much has been made by the Government, and in particular the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), about the effectiveness of this board. Since the board is the only mechanism in the legislation to control future increases in the price of pharmaceuticals, it is important, in my view, to have a very close examination of the board's validity.
The powers given to the board are set out in subsection 41.15(2) of Bill C-22 as follows:
The Board may revoke the patent protection (exclusivity period) of an "excessively priced" drug as well as one other drug under patent by that patentee; or
The Board may cause the price of the "excessively priced" drug to be reduced to such an extent that the maximum price at which the medicine is sold is not excessive.
In my view each of these powers has very serious flaws. I would like to elaborate, for the purposes of this debate and to put them on the record, upon the reasons why 1 believe that the validity of these powers must be questioned.
With respect to the first power given to the board, the power to revoke a drug patent, such power is consistent with the power of the Commissioner of Patents over any other type of patent invention where there has been an abuse of patent privileges.
Unfortunately, however, the additional powers given to the board to revoke a patent on one other drug of the patentee is a power not given to the commissioner over any other patented invention or patent holder. This makes the legislation discriminatory in the sense that one group of patent holders, those
holding pharmaceutical patents, is treated differently from other groups of patent holders, those holding other patented products or processes.
This may be contrary to Section 15 of the Charter which guarantees equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination. Furthermore, it could be argued that such sanctions constitute cruel and unusual treatment or punishment contrary to Section 12 of the Charter.
With respect to the second power given to the board, the power to fix a price at which a drug may be sold, this power as well raises a fundamental issue of constitutionality. By virtue of subsection 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1982, the provinces are given the exclusive jurisdiction to make laws in relation to property and civil rights in the province. "Property and civil rights in the province" encompasses the whole range of legal rights between persons, including law relating to property, succession, the family, torts and contracts.
I pointed out earlier that it is my opinion that at the first instance when a company is called into question and the powers of the board are attempted to be utilized, the company will say that it is unconstitutional. Thereby, the effectiveness of the board will be put into question. It will take innumerable time in order for decisions to be made. The case will be protracted for a considerable time, thus enabling the situation to fester.
The price at which goods are sold is a matter to be decided between two persons. That is private law as opposed to a matter governing the relationship between a person and an institution of Government. It is therefore clearly a provincial matter.
I can assure the House that the multinational corporations will waste no time when a sanction is imposed upon them by this board to place it before the Federal Court in order to have its jurisdiction and authority questioned.
The extent of provincial jurisdiction over pricing was questioned in the famous anti-inflation reference case referred to the Supreme Court of Canada and decided in 1976.
The Anti-Inflation Act, 1975, on which the reference was based, instituted a program of wage and price controls to be administered by a federal tribunal. The scheme was temporary and the Act automatically expired at the end of 1978.
The Supreme Court of Canada held, by a majority of seven to two, that the Act was valid as an exercise of the federal Government residual emergency power. There was no question that the intent of the Act was indeed an excursion into an exclusive matter of the provinces, namely property and civil rights. However, the incursion was justified by Mr. Chief Justice Laskin as being a rational basis which was temporarily necessary to meet a situation of economic crisis imperilling the well-being of Canada as a whole and requiring Parliament's stern intervention in the interest of the country as a whole.
May 1, 1987

Clearly, the situation of the Patented Medicine Review Board is not the equivalent of what Chief Justice Bora Laskin said in the Supreme Court of Canada with regard to this particular matter.
This is a subject matter that comes under the provincial jurisdiction. This is not an emergency situation. It does not come to a conclusion within 16 to 20 months, but exists for an indefinite time.
On those three grounds alone, the courts are apt to strike down the constitutionality of this particular review board, thereby enabling multinational corporations which are in violation of the spirit and the law as it pertains to Bill C-22 to slip away in the darkness of the night or the brightness of the day because the Government refuses to acknowledge that this is wrong.
I know that Members opposite agree. I know that the majority of Members in the House want to support me on this amendment, but we know that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazan-kowski), and of course "Gucci-Gucci", the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), have made a deal with the United States, based on the auspices of free trade, that this legislation will go through.
Mir. Orlikow: Mr. Speaker, my Motion No. 23, if adopted, will tighten the price control provisions of this Bill. The Government has always implied that price control means that all drug prices will increase at the inflation rate. However, the Manitoba Government and others have pointed out that present price control criteria would justify any price increase, including those as high as 140 per cent. This amendment would tighten the criteria to increases of the industry's sales price index, not the CPI, which is a retail index for wholesale cost increases. Since the Government is pretending that it is giving inflation-only increases, then this amendment should be accepted.
I have already quoted from testimony given last week before a United States House of Representatives subcommittee looking at this whole question. It indicated that in the last six years the price of prescription drugs in the United States has gone up by over 79 per cent. That is substantially higher than the increase in the cost of living in that country. The same will happen here.
I also pointed out earlier that in the next few years we will face a host of new prescription drugs that will be brought on the market. While some of them will involve new processes that will give us better drugs, others will be modifications of present drugs so that the companies can charge higher prices. Despite all the arguments we have heard, the Government has used its power to force this Bill through Parliament at every stage. It has done so primarily because it knows how much opposition there is against the Bill.

I know. The Conference of Catholic Bishops, copycat drug companies.

The editorial concludes:

And who's going to blow the whistle when the multinational drug companies don't live up to their glowing promises but continue to do their research and development in the U.S., Britain and Europe where their head offices are located? . .. profits have not suffered unduly under generic competition.

If members on the government side do not want to listen to the editorials, let me quote a letter that was sent to the Minister by the President of Keystone Agricultural Producers, an organization in Manitoba which takes in all the farm commodity groups. The President of Keystone Agriculture Producers, Jack Penner, is a very good friend of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). I am told he has worked for and supported the Minister. Let me put on the record what Mr. Penner, on behalf of Keystone Agricultural Producers, said in a letter he wrote to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre). He wrote:
The KAP's concerns about the proposed amendments are twofold. Firstly, and most obviously, KAP members share the concerns of those who believe that extended patent protections, will, by limiting the ability of drug manufacturing companies to produce generic copies by means of royalty payments, raise the prices charged to consumers for pharmaceutical drugs to unwarranted levels. Farmers and their families are, of course, part of the general consuming public, and stand to be seriously affected in any such situation.

Secondly, since many of the drug manufacturing companies which produce pharmaceutical drugs are the same companies which produce the chemical formulations used by agricultural producers in the production of primary food commodities, it is our belief that any measures which may be taken with respect to pharmaceutical drugs may have significant implications with respect to the production and pricing of pesticides.

Member from Ontario wants to get up and speak, I invite him to do so, because every time he opens his mouth and puts something on the record, he demonstrates again and again his ignorance, his prejudice and his lack of concern about people in western Canada and particularly farmers who are really suffering.
I say to the Hon. Member and to other members of the Government that instead of listening to the pleas of the pharmaceutical manufacturers, the multinational corporations, whose profits have been as high or higher than any other group in this country, instead of listening to their pleas and giving them everything they want, the Government ought to listen to the pleas and arguments of the hundreds of organizations, churches, community groups, labour groups, consumer groups and farm groups, all of whom have urged the Government to withdraw this Bill and to continue with the present legislation.
The Minister asks us to look at the public opinion polls. All the public opinion polls except the poll commissioned by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association, with a question it drafted-which was completely distorted-showed that the public is opposed to this Bill, and when the public gets a chance to vote in the next election, they will show the Government what they really think.

REMEMBRANCE OF INNOCENT VICTIMS Mr. W. Paul McCrossan (York-Scarborough) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of designating the period from April 19 to April 24 each year as a period of remembrance in Canada of innocent civilian victims of violence and terrorism.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion M-41 is a deceptively simple motion, but one which I believe warrants the support of the whole House because it tries to achieve several objectives.
In Canada there should be an annual focus in Parliament on those currently the victims of persecution based on race, religion, national origin, or political affiliation, as well as victims of terrorism so that public opinion can be mobilized to protect potential victims. This is particularly relevant today when, as a result of spurious refugee claims, Canadians are claiming the refugee process. We must systematically take the opportunity to highlight situations of genuine persecution which warrant refugee treatment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Violence and Terrorism
Of course, we could designate any time of the year as the period in which to focus on human rights abuses. My motion on the Order Paper suggests that the specific period between April 19 and April 24 be chosen. These dates, in the third week of April, were deliberately chosen because of historical events which took place this century. In my opinion, the decision to designate a national day of remembrance for victims of man's inhumanity to man can best be given historical relevance by directly relating the remembrance day to the horrible events of the recent past.
During the First World War, between one-half and two-thirds of the Armenian population died as a result of measures taken in the Ottoman Empire commencing with the order for the arrest of the first leaders of the Armenian community on April 24, 1915. In the area which is now northeastern Turkey and Soviet Armenia, Armenians reacted with resistance in response to those arrests. The resistance was quickly and forcefully crushed with many reprisals against the community. However, reprisals did not end there. The Armenian population was first put into concentration camps and then forcefully relocated from their home territory, during which time hundreds of thousands died from starvation, from attacks by the civilian population or at the hands of their government guards. The Armenians were the only race during the First World War subject to such proportionately massive losses. Indeed, within a decade, the term genocide was first used specifically to describe the large scale elimination of a people specifically with respect to the Armenian tragedy during the First World War.
It is important to recognize that while this represented the first major genocide in the 20th century, the concept of racially motivated killings unfortunately did not originate at that time nor has it ceased since. Shortly after the First World War, millions of Ukrainians were systematically starved by Stalin. Before the First World War, during the break-up of the Ottoman Empire in the so-called Balkan wars, there were all too many documented instances of entire villages being killed in the most horrible ways imaginable, including many villages of ethnic Turks. We should, of course, condemn these racially motivated killings as well.
During the First World War, the number of Turks who died as a result of starvation and war also reached into the hundreds of thousands. However, what distinguishes the Armenian tragedy from all others in World War I is that the vast majority of the civilian deaths occurred after the people had been rounded up for relocation by the governmental authorities of the Ottoman Empire and were specially under government protection. This should not be forgotten.
The second date mentioned in the motion, that of April 19, was chosen because on April 19, 1943, the Warsaw ghetto uprising commenced. Through the work of Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Elie Wiesel, we now have an annual commemoration of the Holocaust based on this date, although it is frequently celebrated by Jews throughout the world as occurring on the 27th of Nisan, the equivalent date on the Jewish calendar. All
of us are aware of the millions of innocent civilians, particularly Jews, who died in the Nazi concentration camps in the most systematic, barbaric attempt at racial annihilation the world has ever seen. In the Holocaust, the European Jewish population suffered the largest proportionate losses of any race in the Second World War.
It is, therefore, appropriate to select the date for annually recognizing human rights violations to civilians close to the dates symbolic of the most tragic events of each world war.
Moreover, these two events are connected in another bizarre way. It has been reported, when Hitler was challenged concerning his plans for the Jews, that he said, "Who now remembers the Armenians?" As a result of these reports, there have periodically been efforts by both the Armenian and Jewish populations to point out that lack of action by the world community to the First World War Armenian killings facilitated the path for Hitler during the Second World War. Some historians challenge the remarks attributed to Hitler as apocryphal. Whether apocryphal or not, the fact is that the world community had indeed largely forgotten the lessons of the First World War and that Hitler proceeded with his systematic racial extermination plans.
Following the Second World War, in reaction to the racially motivated mass killings of civilians, steps were taken both to define genocide and other war crimes and to ensure that sanctuary would, in future, be available for genuine refugees fleeing for their lives by establishing the U.N. High Commission on Refugees and the Geneva Convention on Refugees.
However, in the last two decades we have begun again to see an escalation of persecution and terrorism with victims, based on race, religion, national origin or political conviction, such as the Bahai's in Iran, the Miskito Indians in Nicaragua and Guatemala, and supporters of President Allende in Chile. The Pot Pol regime has killed millions in Kampuchea. We have also seen the starvation and indiscriminate killings of men, women and children in the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps in Beirut by both Christians and Shiites, the murders of thousands of Sikhs in India following Mrs. Gandhi's assassination, the murders of Hindu men, women and children travelling on buses in the Punjab, the bombings and shootings of hundreds of bus passengers in Sri Lanka, the bombings of civilians in villages in Afghanistan, terrorist attacks against civilians in Israel, and most pertinent to Canada, the deaths of 329 innocent passengers on Air-India Flight 182.
Some of these events represent state terrorism, others represent terrorism by groups who seek to change the political order. Still others, such as the recent death of a guard at the Turkish Embassy in Ottawa, represent attacks by isolated individuals who believe that terrorism is justified in the name of history. Canada is a world leader in the struggle for human rights. We should, therefore, also be a leader in ensuring that events in which civilians are killed as a result of state terrorism, group terrorism or individual terrorism, are condemned and, where possible, that world-wide remedial steps are taken.
May 1, 1987

I understand that there will be an amendment to my motion moved during the debate to select the first Monday of the third week of April as the date of remembrance in order to secularize the motion to cover all violence to civilians in all countries. I hope this will lead to a formal annual parliamentary statement.
I wish to indicate that the amendment is acceptable to me provided that it is clearly on the record that the choice of this date is designed to centre the day of remembrance between the specific dates mentioned in my motion.
This is important because there are some people in the world who now attempt to deny that the tragic events in the First World War and the Second World War referred to in my motion happened at all. Indeed, we have all recently seen two trials in Canada concerning the distribution of such hate literature. By passage of this motion, the Parliament of Canada would be stating unequivocally that it recognizes that the First World War Armenian genocide and the Second World War Holocaust are indisputable historical facts.
In summary, through the passage of this motion, I believe that Canada can provide a lead to the world by ensuring that similar events in the future are publicized and that corrective international action is started expeditiously. As such, I view the passage of my motion as both complementary to and a logical extension of the work done by Elie Wiesel in focusing on the Holocaust so that the lessons of the past can be applied to prevent future tragedies.

The presence of this motion on the Order Paper today has been a causal event in my life, but it has caused me to reflect on my last few years in Parliament and the extent of knowledge that I have about the degree to which violence and terrorism was a daily fact of life in many countries of the world. It was not very great the day I was first elected to this Chamber. To that extent, I think I share the state of knowledge that exists for a great many Canadians. I might even go so far as to say that such is the case perhaps for most Canadians.
I happen to be a fourth generation Canadian. When I reflect on family history, I think again I am not unlike many Canadians who have moved into the fourth, fifth and sixth generation,
Violence and Terrorism
but our ancestors came to this country in most, if not all cases, to escape violence, terrorism and persecution. We are a nation whose future to a large extent has been conditioned by that reality. Out of those kinds of experiences comes our special feeling for democracy, for the kinds of things that are important to this Chamber, important to our electoral process and important to our ways of governing ourselves.
I have had the honour to represent this Government for 11 weeks of the 1984 Fall Assembly of the United Nations. There are less than 40 democracies in an assembly of something in excess of 160 countries that are either full members or are represented there.
A true democracy is a very special commodity. I think we have special responsibilities in the world. It is appropriate that as a nation we set aside a day which gives us a focus and reason for coming together. It gives fourth generation Canadians a reason for remembering our history and our roots. What does it give more current first generation Canadians who came to the country as refugees, escaping the persecution and terrorism to which the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough referred? For them those memories are fresh. They have certain knowledge of friends and relatives who still exist in situations where there is real, genuine, and well-founded fear of persecution, of terrorism, and of violence.
I hope we as a nation will applaud the efforts of Parliament to set aside that kind of day. Then, as the future unfolds, hopefully we will put some effort into deciding the kinds of remembrances which would be appropriate on that special day.
We need to be reminded that the price of peace is also vigilance. When it comes to human rights, the need to be vigilant is ever present. There is a tendency in the busyness of our lives and our daily existence to forget that. Anything we as a Parliament and a nation can do to ensure that we do not forget it should be done, so that we remain conscious of it and responsive to it. This would speak well of us as a people and as a nation.
It is with a great deal of pleasure that I should like to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), the following:
That the words "the period from April 19 to April 24" be deleted and that the words "the third Monday in April" be substituted in their place.
The effect of this amendment would be to secularize the motion by providing a specific day each year for the remembrance to take place. Therefore the motion, as amended, would read:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of designating the third Monday in April each year as a period of remembrance in Canada of innocent civilian victims of violence and terrorism.

I have always been in favour of stating the facts as they are, very clearly, specifically and publicly. A number of consultations took place among Hon. Members and among various groups, including the Canadian Armenian Community, and I am sure other Members consulted with the Canadian community of Jewish faith, there is no doubt. Personally I like this kind of resolution, of motion and of commemoration because a people without memory does not deserve to survive. But I am somewhat embarrassed because the people who are primarily concerned and whom we would like to help have expressed-at least most of them did-their disagreement with the motion as drafted. I for one wish that some day people will be able to remember, but if we want to remember the least we can expect is that all those people for whom we want to remember should be in agreement. This is nothing new for me, Mr. Speaker. In April 1989-I see the Hon. Member listening attentively, my NDP colleague, I have him in mind today when I mention related issues of this story. In April 1989 it will be 25 years since, like many others, I began to familiarize myself with the Armenian community. In fact, it was in April 1964, I think it will be twenty-five years ago in 1989, and this is the twenty-fifth time I have raised this issue. It is one of my year-round concerns, but even more so on April 24.
What worries the Armenian community is this refusal to want to have something that reminds the world and Canadians of those events. If the House can accept the Hon. Member's amendment that does away with the date April 19, that is all right and we agree.

We agree that one of the great tragedies of the world occurred on April 19, 1943, the day when the Warsaw uprising began. It is commemorated as Holocaust Remembrance Day. Some day-and that day is coming soon-I will talk about my view of the Holocaust, this great world atrocity.
However, contained in the motion of the Hon. It is considered to be-and we cannot change history; we cannot accommodate history-the beginning of the Armenian genocide. The Armenian community would have preferred at least part of the resolution put forward by the Hon. Member, but certainly not the amendment. They also have great reservations about le libelle de la resolution as it read then and as it reads now.
I have talked directly with the Hon. Member who moved the motion. I am trying to be fair to him, but I am also trying to reflect the strong views which have been put forward to me.
I wonder whether we could show Parliament at its best today. It is only an idea. The Hon. Member knows that I have been agonizing about what I will finally do. However, April has passed. We have almost 11 months to wait until next April. We want to remember the Holocaust. I sincerely do. We want to remember the genocide. I sincerely do, as does the Hon. Member. However, some people are already debating the way we are going to do it. I wonder whether that is the correct way to do it.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to have the opportunity to represent the New Democratic Party in the debate on the
Violence and Terrorism
motion introduced by the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) and its amendment. In considering the justification for the motion, I suppose one can be reflective about the fact that this motion addresses itself to violence and genocide in the 20th century, but I am not too sure why that should necessarily be so.
I know that Thomistic and Aristotelian philosophy, when trying to come to grips with that which distinguishes man from other animals, defined human beings as being rational animals. We could suppose that the 20th century is focused upon rationality because I think many of us consider it to be the rational century, the century during which man has achieved the highest stage yet achieved in his development and the pursuit of the fulfilment of that ancient definition. Today we are dealing with those instances in which man has not done violence merely to fellow man but to himself and his very essence, the times when man has been reduced to the level of the animal, to the most primitive stage of man's evolution.
Humanity is unique as a species. As a biologist, I know it to be rare for a species to attack its own members. There are no wars among most species and there is no terrorism among most species. There is no genocide among any of them.
While we focus upon the 20th century, much of that with which we are concerned today represents a legacy of the 19th century. I stand as a descendant of a people who lost many; slaves who were shipped from Africa to the new world. It is not well known that far more slaves died during slavery than died in the 20th century Holocaust. We might reflect upon the fate of the Indians of South America, of the victims of colonialism throughout the world, of man's inhumanity to man.
I am not sure that I quite understand all of what is implied by my Liberal friend's intervention, but surely it is clear that the Armenian genocide and the Holocaust represent more than significant events in the 20th century. They represent new legacies and illustrate all the more in this rational century just how necessary it is for us to be concerned about the tendency of human beings to lose their character and kill because of race, religion or politics, to kill sporadically, randomly, in the form of terrorism to achieve some purpose which in their minds justifies acting like animals.
As we reflect upon the Armenian genocide, however worthy it is of commemoration, and it is; as we reflect upon the Holocaust, however worthy of commemoration it is, and it is; we must not forget that even as we stand here there may be another bomb being planted among a civilian population somewhere in the world. There may be another slaughter of passengers on a bus in Sri Lanka. There may be more Miskito Indians being slaughtered in Central America. Genocide has not ended. Violence has not ended. When we talk about the reduction of man to animalistic viciousness, let us not forget it is our rationality in the form of technology that all too often makes it possible to contemplate and justify so-called higher purposes violence of a sort that would never be contemplated as being included in the definition contained in this motion, violence in the form of nuclear or chemical warfare.

It is more than worth-while, indeed more than necessary, that there be a commemoration of those two fatal events, one for the Armenians and the other for the Jews. However, that commemoration must not be regarded as limited to those two tragedies. It must be directed to the prevention of any new tragedies. It would do us little good, however we do it, to commemorate these two events and ignore the images on television last night which sound the clarion call of warning to the world that a new genocide is about to be perpetrated upon the people of Mozambique.
Who would see the blood spewing from the mouth of a starving dying child, knowing it is the result of the activity of a regime whose view of mankind is completely contradictory to the view represented in this motion and, failing to act, not know that nothing has been learned from the Armenian genocide and the Jewish Holocaust?
Therefore, if this motion is adopted, in whatever form it might be adopted, and I hope it will be, nothing will be accomplished if it does not communicate to us and every other democratic country in the world that wherever there is racism, wherever there is antipathy on the basis of religion, wherever there is intolerance of differing political views, there is the possibility of new terrorism and new genocide. That is the message I know and understand, indeed the message that is intended to be communicated by the Hon. Member for York-Scarborough and this House when it adopts this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate this afternoon. As you know, we have always held on Friday afternoons debates that are very interesting for Members who choose to spend their Friday afternoon here rather than elsewhere. We often have an opportunity to share opinions, feelings and hopes on matters of importance to a large number of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, like many of my colleagues I have received a letter dated April 2, 1987, from Mr. M. Hagopian, Chairman of the National Armenian Committee of Canada.

The letter Mr. Hagopian sent reads as follows:
Motion M-41, introduced by Mr. Paul McCrossan, M.P. for York-
Scarborough, has been drawn as a non-votable motion.
April 10, 1987, has been tentatively set as a date for consideration of M-41 by
the House of Commons.
As my colleague indicated, that date was changed and that explains why a number of my colleagues, particularly the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and the Hon. Member for Outremont (Mrs.. Pepin), who desperately wanted to speak on this motion, are unable to be with us today. It is the fault of no one, just the fact that the date was changed. The letter continues:
It is our understanding, that Mr. McCrossan's intention is setting a special remembrance period for the victims of all genocides. Hence, the selection of the dates.
April 19, 1943, is the day when the Warsaw uprising began and is commemorated as Holocaust Remembrance Day;
April 24, 1915, is the date of the mass arrests of the Armenian leadership in Istanbul, Turkey, and is considered to be the beginning of the Armenian Genocide.
Of course, the remembrance period would not be exclusively for the victims of the Jewish Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide, since, unfortunately, other genocides were committed in this century as well.
Furthermore, this would be an appropriate time each year for Parliament to focus on the present-day universal problem of persecution based on race, religion, or national origin.
As you would probably conclude from reading this page it appears that Mr. Hagopian was in favour of the motion. However, let me read to you the second page and you will see that there is a problem with the text of the motion as originally presented and, I submit, a further problem with the amendment brought to our attention today should it be passed. He continues:
However, the language of Mr. McCrossan's motion does not reflect his purpose, and it is vague and ambiguous. M-41 does not address the concerns of the Canadian Armenian community, and some might even consider it to be an affront to the memory of those who perished. Nonetheless, we sincerely believe that Mr. McCrossan is well-intentioned.
In order to directly and clearly address the issue, we suggest that the last words of M-41 "violence and terrorism," be replaced by "genocide and mass extermination," or "war crimes and crimes against humanity".
We strongly urge you to express our views when M-41 is debated in the House. We count on your understanding and support. Your co-operation will be very much appreciated.
There is quite a simple explanation for why Mr. Hagopian wrote such a letter. When I first read the letter I thought it was unusual that a person would initially express support and then reluctance. I referred to documents which I have and others which my colleagues provided to me and found the answer.
On July 23, 1984, during the last election campaign a Member of Parliament of the Progressive Conservative Party promised that a day would be set aside as a day of remembrance for the estimated 1.5 million Armenians killed during the Ottoman massacre of 1915. That was, of course, the Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), a senior member of the then opposition Tory caucus.
I believe that the Armenian community interprets the motion before the House today as an attempt by the Government to fulfil that commitment. However, it does not go nearly far enough to fulfil the original commitment made by that Party. The amendment of the Hon. Member from Calgary removes completely the date of April 24, and I am sure that members of the Armenian community will not be satisfied with the amended motion, if it passes, especially considering they were not entirely satisfied with the original motion.

They did, however, highly praise the Member for York Scarborough (Mr. McCrossan) who brought the matter to the attention of the House. I believe, as does my colleague from Saint-Denis and Mr. Hagopian, that the Member for York-Scarborough had only good intentions in the original motion.
I was hoping that the amendment of the Member from Calgary would have reflected the proposals of Mr. Hagopian in his letter of April 2, 1987, which he sent to many Members of Parliament. I surveyed a number of my colleagues who all said they had received it, so presumably all Members of this House, including the Member from Calgary who moved the amendment, must have been aware of Mr. Hagopian's concern.
Why was the amendment moved to water down the motion when Mr. Hagopian wanted it strengthened because it did not fulfil the commitment made by the Conservative Party in 1984? I hope all Members of this House will take note of that concern.
We know that the Government is not famous for keeping its promises made during the election campaign of 1984. I do not want to go through the whole litany of promises which it broke. I have done that on sufficient occasions in this House. However, if provoked I would gladly raise them again.

parties have an opportunity to express their views and examine the substance of the motion.
Motion 41 put forward by my colleague from the Conservative Party says:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of designating the period from April 19 to April 24 each year as a period of remembrance in Canada of innocent civilian victims of violence and terrorism.
The amendment changes the time to the third week in May. It is worth noting that parliamentarians have the opportunity to send a very significant signal to individual Canadians who have relatives or friends who have been the victims of such violence and terrorism. On that note I want to congratulate my colleague from the Conservative Party because I think that is his intention.
I specifically want to address my remarks to the Holocaust. Three weeks ago I had the opportunity to speak with some young people from Halifax. We spoke about the issue of the Soviet Jewery and the difficulties with which people in that country are still plagued. It is rather frightening when you study history, view films, listen to commentary of various individuals, and read reports of Parliament to learn what some individuals were confronted with at a very difficult time in our history. These young people impressed me because they wanted, as I am sure the Hon. Member opposite wants, to highlight in a real way the significance of the Holocaust and other acts of violence and terrorism.
While the Hon. Member has his idea, these young people gave me other suggestions. Perhaps from time to time Parliament would put away its partisanship and discuss issues of international importance for a day or two when the Chamber could perhaps adopt a resolution that is agreeable to all Parties and, more important, to those individuals who are directly involved.
In this way Canada as a nation and as a free people could send a signal domestically and internationally that Canada is concerned, remembers, and has the compassion to make sure that the events of the past will never reoccur in the future.
They also suggested that this debate should not only consist of national leaders but also of Members of Parliament from all Parties who could espouse their views and those of their constituents so that Canadians would gain a better appreciation for what I believe is a well-intended motion.
All too often, we have a tendency in the country to forget. I do not say that because I believe anyone wants to forget past events in world history intentionally, but that is what happens as time and the world go on.

I believe that parliamentarians, particularly at the federal level, although I mean no disrespect to provincial parliamentarians, have an obligation to address this issue.
The students also said that while it is important to debate in the House of Commons and pass a resolution, perhaps we must do more. The original suggestion in the Hon. Member's motion was to set aside April 19 to April 24 for this remembrance. That has been amended to the third week of May. My colleague, the Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has a profound interest in this subject, as I am sure all Members of Parliament do. I know that he would have preferred to be here if it were possible.
Perhaps some national organizations, as referred to by my colleague who spoke before me, may not share or fully appreciate the pith and substance of the motion that the Member is putting forward today. I have a letter that I believe all Members of Parliament received from the Armenian National Committee of Canada. 1 would like to quote from that letter because they make some interesting observations. It states:
April 10, 1987, has been tentatively set as a date for consideration of M-41 by the House of Commons.

April 24, 1915, is the date of the mass arrests of the Armenian leadership in Istanbul, Turkey, and is considered to be the beginning of the Armenian Genocide.
Of course, the remembrance period would not be exclusively for the victims of the Jewish Holocaust and the Armenian Genocide, since, unfortunately, other genocides were committed in this century as well. Furthermore, this would be an appropriate time each year for Parliament to focus on the present-day universal problem of persecution based on race, religion, or national origin.
I am not taking issue with the Armenian National Committee of Canada, but I want to say as a parliamentarian that we cannot set aside only one day or have just one debate. It cannot consist of one speech given by a government Minister and responded to by an opposition Member. My hon. colleague opposite has suggested a period of time for reflection on what has taken place.
The letter goes on:
However, the language of Mr. McCrossan's motion does not reflect his purpose, and it is vague and ambiguous.
I am not sure I necessarily agree with that, but I suggest that this provides an opportunity, particularly for the Hon.
Member opposite and my colleague, the Member for Laval-des-Rapides, for consultations with some of these organizations.
I congratulate the Member opposite for introducing this motion and allowing for this debate. I think his motion has a lot of substance which deserves reflection by all Members of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, in the two or three minutes remaining I want to associate myself with the Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) who gave his support to the intent of this resolution.
I am not too concerned about the number of days because in the 20th century we have become successful in many areas and can do more than we have ever done in the world.
It is also obvious that we can kill more people than ever before. Mention has been made of the genocide of the Armenians in Turkey and of the Holocaust when six million Jews were killed by the Nazis.
We ought to remember the more recent times, with the deaths of four million people in Cambodia. We should remember the Idi Amin regime in Uganda, the civil war in Nigeria when the people in the Biafra province tried to separate from Nigeria, and the killings taking place in Sri Lanka at the present time.
There is the tragedy in Ireland. We cannot forget the events since World War I in the Soviet Union with the death by starvation of five million or six million Ukrainian people and the purges and wars which took place. It was estimated by the son of one of the leaders of the Communist uprising in 1917 that sixty million people living in the Soviet Union have died since then. So we say that violence and terrorism are a part, tragically, of the 20th century. We accept the proposal of the Hon. Member that we should remember this and honour these people wherever that happens.
